questions.q: What is the central message about trust that the story conveys through Anil's behaviour toward Hari?
questions.a: The story shows that trust, even when seemingly naive, can catalyse moral transformation; Anil's unwavering trust — giving Hari a key, ignoring the theft — ultimately awakens Hari's conscience. A wrong answer (e.g., "Anil is foolish to trust a thief") reveals the student views trust as weakness rather than a deliberate, redemptive choice the author validates.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Hari's decision to return the money demonstrates redemption, and why the timing (at the railway station) matters.
questions.a: Redemption is Hari's conscious choice to reject his old identity; returning the money at the station — the threshold of escape — proves the change is internal, not forced by circumstance. A wrong answer that says "he returned it because he feared getting caught" shows the student confuses external consequence with internal moral agency, a common board-exam error.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "transformative power of education" to a new situation: If Anil had only fed and sheltered Hari without teaching him to read/write, would Hari still have returned the money? Justify using textual logic.
questions.a: No — the text explicitly links Hari's return to his realization that "whole sentences could... bring me more than a few hundred rupees." Without literacy, Hari sees no alternative future; education provides the vision that makes honesty rational. A wrong answer that claims "yes, because Anil was kind" misses the causal link the author builds between literacy and long-term self-interest.

questions.q: Analyze how the three themes interact in the final paragraph where Anil hands Hari a fifty-rupee note, saying, "I made some money yesterday... you'll be paid regularly."
questions.a: The fifty-rupee note symbolizes restored trust (Anil pays despite knowing), completed redemption (Hari earns honestly), and education's payoff (regular income from a skill). A wrong answer that treats the note as mere payment fails to see the triple thematic convergence the author engineers in one gesture.

questions.q: Evaluate the criticism: "Anil's trust is irresponsible; a real teacher would have reported Hari to the police." Defend or refute using the story's moral framework.
questions.a: Refute: The story operates on a moral, not legal, framework. Anil's "irresponsible" trust is the precise catalyst that saves Hari; reporting him would reinforce criminal identity. A wrong answer that agrees with the criticism imposes external legalism on a text designed to show compassion's efficacy — a misreading that loses board marks for missing authorial intent.

questions.q: Create a 50-word diary entry from Hari's perspective the night he returns the money, weaving in all three themes without naming them directly.
questions.a: A strong entry shows Hari's voice, mentions the key, the unwritten sentences, the train's whistle, and the wet notes — e.g., "The key feels heavier than the bundle. I couldn't read the station sign, but I read Anil's face when he taught me. The notes are damp; my hands are clean." A weak entry lists themes abstractly ("I learned trust") instead of dramatizing them.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Theme is the central idea or underlying message that a literary work conveys about human experience; in "The Thief's Story," the intertwined themes of trust, redemption, and the ______ power of education are developed through Hari Singh's journey from a habitual thief to a boy who chooses honesty because he values learning over stolen money.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are Hari Singh, holding a bundle of stolen notes at the ______ station, the train to Lucknow about to leave — yet you turn back.
What is Theme? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Theme is the central idea or underlying message that a literary work conveys about human experience; in "The Thief's Story," the intertwined themes of trust, redemption, and the transformative power of education are developed through Hari Singh's journey from a habitual thief to a boy who chooses honesty because he values learning over.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Theme?
questions.a: Students often write that Hari returns the money solely because he fears Anil will discover the theft, ignoring the textual evidence that Anil *already knows* (wet notes) and says nothing.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify textual evidence for each of the three themes, explain how they interconnect in Hari's character arc, and write a structured board-exam answer using the PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) method with at least two well-chosen quotations or textual references per theme.
